opus-5.5.text:
I think the starting point for me is pretty simple: it's your data. It's information about your body, your history, your life, and for a long time the reality has been that it's scattered across a dozen different portals, a few PDFs, maybe a fax somewhere, and the person it's actually about is often the one with the least practical access to it. So when we think about what something like ChatGPT Health should enable, a big part of it is just helping people actually use the information that already belongs to them.

Concretely, that means a few things. One is bringing it together. If you can connect your records, your lab results, maybe data from a wearable or an app you already use, then you can ask questions with real context instead of starting from zero every time. "Is this cholesterol number something I should worry about?" is a very different question when the model can see your trend over five years, your medications, and your family history, versus answering in the abstract.

The second piece is understanding. A lot of people get a lab report or a visit summary and it's essentially written in a language they don't speak. Helping someone understand what they're looking at, what questions to bring to their next appointment, what's routine versus what deserves a follow-up, that's empowering in a way that I think makes the relationship with their clinician better, not worse. You walk in more prepared, and the time with your doctor goes further.

And then the third piece, which I think has to be non-negotiable, is control. Ownership isn't real if you can't decide who sees what, and if you can't take it back. So people should be able to choose what they connect, see what's being used, disconnect things, and delete things. Health conversations should be treated with an extra layer of protection and separation, and they shouldn't be used to train models by default. People are sharing some of the most sensitive things in their lives, and the bar for trust has to be correspondingly high. If we don't earn that, none of the rest matters.

I'd also say that we try to be really clear about what this is and isn't. It's not meant to replace your care team. It's meant to help you be a more informed, more engaged participant in your own care. Some of the most meaningful stories we hear are from people who caught something, or pushed for a second opinion, or finally understood a diagnosis they'd been living with for years, because they could actually engage with their own information. That's the vision: your data, working for you, under your control.

r001.rationale: The response says patients often have the least practical access to records scattered across portals, but does not state that their data was shared despite that lack of access.

r002.rationale: It describes patients becoming more informed and prepared to engage in their care, including pushing for a second opinion, which communicates self-advocacy.

r003.rationale: It proposes bringing scattered records together so patients can use them with real context, communicating reduced effort to access and use their data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the starting point for me is that patients have always, in principle, owned their health data, but in practice they've had almost no ability to actually use it. You have a right to your records under HIPAA, but what that's looked like for most people is a patient portal they log into once a year, a PDF of lab results they can't interpret, and a bunch of information scattered across five different health systems that don't talk to each other. So ownership has been kind of nominal. The data is technically yours, but it's not legible to you, and it's not portable in any meaningful sense.

What I think ChatGPT Health should enable is making that ownership real. And I'd break that into a couple of pieces.

The first is that you should be able to bring your data to the model. If you want to connect your medical records, your wearable data, your lab history, that should be something you choose to do, and it should be something you can undo. You should be able to see what's connected, disconnect it, delete it. That control has to sit with the person, not with the health system or with us.

The second piece is that once the data is there, the value should flow back to you. The thing people actually want isn't a dashboard of their biomarkers. It's answers to questions like, "Is this normal for me?" or "What should I ask my doctor about on Thursday?" or "I've had three visits for this same thing, what's the pattern?" A model that has your context can do that in a way that a generic search can't, and that's really the whole point of having your own data accessible to you. It's not just about possession, it's about being able to reason over it.

The third thing, and this is where I think we have to be really careful, is that the trust model has to match the sensitivity of the data. Health information is probably the most sensitive data most people have. So we've been pretty deliberate that conversations in Health aren't used to train models, that there's a clear separation from the rest of someone's ChatGPT usage, and that the defaults err on the side of privacy. I think if you get that wrong even once, you lose the ability to do any of the good stuff.

And then I'd just add, I think there's a broader shift happening where the locus of care is moving a bit, from being purely something that happens to you inside an institution to something you can participate in more actively between visits. Clinicians are still central, and I don't think anything we build should try to replace that relationship. But most of someone's health happens outside the fifteen minutes they get with a doctor. If people can actually understand and use their own information in those other ten thousand hours, that's a pretty meaningful change, and it's one that I think should be designed around the patient from the start rather than retrofitted later.

r001.rationale: The response says patients struggled to use their records and that data was scattered across health systems, but it does not state that others had access to the data while patients lacked practical access.

r002.rationale: It describes using personal health context to prepare questions for a doctor and participate more actively in care, which communicates patient self-advocacy.

r003.rationale: It presents ChatGPT Health as letting patients bring scattered records together and get contextual answers, making their data easier to use than portals and generic search.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that patients should have access to and control over their own health information. But access alone isn’t enough. If you get a hundred-page PDF of your medical records and you can’t make sense of it, that’s not really empowering you.

What I’d want ChatGPT Health to enable is for you to bring that information together and understand it: What’s happened over time? What questions should I ask my doctor? What do I still not understand about my treatment options? It should help you become a more informed participant in your care.

And control has to be meaningful. You should be able to decide what you share, what it’s used for, and when to remove it. Health information is incredibly sensitive. The opportunity is to make it useful to the person it belongs to, with clear boundaries and an honest account of what the system can and can’t tell you.

r001.rationale: The response says patients should have access and control, but does not describe the historical asymmetry of health data being shared while patients lacked practical access.

r002.rationale: It says patients can use their information to prepare questions for their doctor and become more informed participants in their care, communicating that access helps them advocate for themselves.

r003.rationale: The response says ChatGPT Health should bring information together and help patients understand it, but does not clearly state that it lowers the effort required to access their health data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is that your health data is yours. You should be able to access it, understand it, and decide how it’s used. But there’s a gap between having access to a portal full of lab results and actually being able to make sense of what’s happening with your health.

What I’d want ChatGPT Health to enable is for you to bring that information together and ask questions in plain language: What does this result mean? How has it changed over time? What should I ask my doctor? It should help you become a more informed participant in your care, with control over what you share and the ability to revoke that access.

The goal is to give people more agency—to make their own information useful to them and help them have better conversations with the clinicians caring for them.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between accessing a portal and understanding health information, but does not say that data was historically shared while patients lacked practical access.

r002.rationale: It mentions agency, informed participation, and better conversations with clinicians, but does not clearly state that access to personal health data enables patients to advocate for themselves.

r003.rationale: It says ChatGPT Health should bring health information together and let patients ask questions in plain language, making their data easier to use.
